groups.name: Dynastinae
groups.description: Rhinoceros beetles form a subfamily of Scarabaeidae. The accounts below document oviposition, larval substrates, seasonal inactivity, and emergence for individual species.

groups.name: Lucanidae
groups.description: Stag beetles (Lucanidae). The account below documents oviposition and larval development in association with decayed hardwood.

groups.name: Rutelinae
groups.description: Shining leaf chafers form a subfamily of Scarabaeidae. These accounts distinguish adult foliage use from the substrates in which larvae develop.

groups.name: Cetoniinae
groups.description: Flower chafers form a subfamily of Scarabaeidae. The species accounts cover adult feeding, oviposition substrate, and pupal-cell formation.

groups.name: Cerambycidae
groups.description: Cerambycidae are longhorn beetles. The two accounts below concern members of Prioninae whose larvae develop in wood or wood-based substrates.

groups.name: Tenebrionidae
groups.description: Darkling beetles (Tenebrionidae). The records below describe captive development from egg to adult.

groups.name: Passalidae
groups.description: Bess beetles (Passalidae) occupy galleries in decaying wood. In the horned passalus, adults and larvae share a gallery and adults provision their offspring.

species.name: Pelidnota punctata
species.intro: Grapevine beetle adults feed on grape foliage. In Kansas, females laid eggs in moist soil beneath decaying logs, and the hatchlings bored into the adjacent wood.

sections.title: Mating and oviposition
sections.text: Field observations in Kansas placed mating adults on wild grape at night. Females laid eggs singly between June 19 and August 17. Fresh eggs measured about 2.0 × 1.5 mm and became rounder as they developed.

sections.title: Development in decaying wood
sections.text: One egg laid in early July 1919 produced an adult on July 11, 1921. In a separate rearing, hatchlings placed in crumbled, decaying elm in July 1920 produced 12 adult males and 17 adult females by July 1922.

sources.title: W. P. Hayes (1925), Kansas Agricultural Experiment Station, Technical Bulletin 16
Angela Miner, Animal Diversity Web, Grapevine beetle
University of Minnesota Extension, Scarab beetles

facts.title: Egg incubation
facts.text: 8–26 days, mean 14.9 days in Kansas laboratory observations

facts.title: Egg to adult
facts.text: Approximately 2 years in a Kansas rearing study

native_status.text: Native to eastern North America, including the eastern United States and southern Canada.

species.name: Odontotaenius disjunctus
species.intro: Both parents tend the brood in galleries excavated in decaying wood. Young adults that remain in the natal log can contribute to the care of later broods.

sections.title: Eggs and larval feeding
sections.text: Adults carry egg clutches between sites within the gallery. After hatching, larvae remain with the parents and feed on softened wood mixed with adult frass. Colonies have been maintained in moist, decayed oak.

sections.title: Pupal chambers
sections.text: Adults pack fragments of wood and other debris around the developing pupae and repair damaged chambers. Both parents and recently emerged adults can construct these cells.

sources.title: C. S. Bibbs and colleagues, UF/IFAS Featured Creatures, Horned passalus

facts.title: Development
facts.text: A single summer in some conditions, up to 14–16 months in others

native_status.text: Native to eastern North America, including the eastern United States and southern Canada. Its range extends west to eastern Texas and the central Great Plains.

species.name: Tenebrio molitor
species.intro: Yellow mealworm larvae feed within cereal substrates. A 2023 rearing study compared oat and wheat by-products and documented the adult breeding period separately from larval growth.

sections.title: Breeding substrate
sections.text: Each breeding tray contained 400 g of grain substrate. Adults oviposited for two weeks before removal, after which the larvae received a further 600 g of substrate. Carrot supplied moisture to both stages.

sections.title: Larval development
sections.text: Larvae grew on either milled oat by-product or wheat bran. The wheat-bran cohort also supplied pupae and adults for the study. Ten weeks was the larval harvest age for analysis.

native_status.text: Introduced and established in North America, including Canada, the United States and Mexico. BugGuide places its North American introduction at approximately 1827.

species.name: Gymnetis thula
species.intro: Adults of the harlequin flower beetle visit flowers and sap flows by day. The same decaying plant material in which females lay their eggs feeds the developing grubs.

sections.title: Adult feeding
sections.text: Adults consume fruit and plant exudates. In Texas, feeding adults have been recorded at sap flows on false willow (Baccharis neglecta).

sections.title: Oviposition and larval habitat
sections.text: Females lay in compost, fermenting oak and other decaying plant material. Larvae have also been found in tree hollows containing decomposed vegetation.

sources.title: Louisiana State University AgCenter, Gymnetis thula, Harlequin Flower Beetle

facts.title: Seasonal activity

species.name: Dynastes tityus
species.intro: Eastern Hercules beetle larvae feed on decaying hardwood, particularly the loose wood debris in cavities at the bases of oaks. Adults have been observed taking sap from wounds on ash trees.

sections.title: Captive reproduction
sections.text: The Kentucky account describes a laying chamber containing at least one US gallon (3.8 L) of moist substrate, with two parts soil to one part decayed hardwood. Adults accepted apple, orange and overripe banana.

sections.title: Seasonal development
sections.text: Females lay eggs in summer. Newly formed adults can remain in their pupal cells through winter and emerge above ground in June or July.

sources.title: Bill Wallin, University of Kentucky Entomology, Rearing Eastern Hercules Beetles
University of Arkansas Arthropod Museum, Eastern Hercules beetle

facts.title: Oviposition
facts.text: Up to 40 eggs per female in a Kentucky captive-rearing account

facts.title: Egg incubation
facts.text: Approximately 1 month under the reported captive conditions

trials.title: Captive breeding observations
trials.intro: A Florida adult series, a separate collection of forest larvae and a historical photograph of a captive-reared male document the species at two life stages.

sections.title: Florida adults
sections.text: The May 2025 Bristol series records the adult male from several angles. The photographs show the shape of the paired horns and the distribution of dark spots on the yellow wing covers.

sections.title: Forest larvae
sections.text: Five larvae were photographed after removal from a forest scheduled for development. The locality was not specified in that report.

sections.title: Horn development
sections.text: A photograph shared in November 2025 shows the largest male the breeder had reared, more than a decade earlier. The breeder remarked on the unusual horn profile of this individual. No length measurement accompanied the photograph.

native_status.text: Native to the eastern United States, from New York south to Florida and west to the eastern Great Plains and eastern Texas.

species.name: Lucanus elaphus
species.intro: In Mississippi floodplain forests, giant stag beetle larvae fed both inside fallen logs and at the boundary between wood and soil. The occupied logs varied in size and type of decay.

sections.title: Oviposition and feeding
sections.text: A published captive account places the eggs in the substrate beside pieces of decayed wood. Larvae developed on either white-rotted wood or fermented substrate.

sections.title: Field observations
sections.text: In Mississippi, larvae tunnelled through wood or fed on its underside where the log rested on soil. Larvae occurred in more than one type of rot.

sources.title: Ulyshen and colleagues (2017), Ecology, genetics and distribution of Lucanus elaphus

species.name: Chrysina woodi
species.intro: Adults accepted foliage of walnuts and hickories in captivity. Late third instars overwintered above a layer of clay, which the larvae used for pupation.

sections.title: Adult feeding and oviposition
sections.text: The account records adults flying along mountain arroyos on cloudy days and at night. Captive adults fed on cut branches of Juglans and Carya, including pecan. Fresh foliage replaced old cuttings every three days. The breeding enclosure contained about 3 in (7.5 cm) of moist, loosely placed flake soil. Adults alternated several days of feeding with periods below the surface during egg laying.

sections.title: Overwintering and pupation
sections.text: The reported method used flake soil or decayed wood for larval development. A layer of clay about 2 in (5 cm) deep was added beneath the substrate for mature third instars. The larvae were kept cool through winter and moved to warmer conditions in spring. Emergence was less synchronous when the winter cooling period was omitted.

sections.title: Adult sex characters
sections.text: In ventral view, females had a fine median line on the terminal abdominal segment. Males showed a dark segment absent in females, according to the account.

sources.title: Breeding Chrysina woodi, the jewel of Texas! (October 19, 2023)

trials.title: First trial · West Texas, 2023
trials.text: I collected four pairs in West Texas and kept two pairs for breeding. One female died within a week of collection. The other lived more than a month and laid 122 eggs in a single clutch. All 122 hatched. I used a well-ventilated enclosure containing about 3.8 L of lightly fermented flake soil and fed the adults hickory leaves. I recommend rearing the larvae individually with red clay for pupation. Development to adulthood took approximately six months.

native_status.text: Native to the mountains of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, including Arizona, New Mexico, western Texas and Chihuahua.

sources.title: New Mexico State Wildlife Action Plan, Wood’s jewel scarab

species.name: Xyloryctes thestalus
species.intro: I reared adults from captive-bred larvae. Only one egg was laid before winter. I found the rest of the eggs and larvae between April and July, after the adults resumed feeding.

sections.title: Breeding substrate
sections.text: I used a ventilated enclosure with 10–13 cm (4–5 in) of lightly fermented flake soil and placed bark on the surface. I kept the substrate slightly moist, drier than I usually keep it for other rhinoceros beetles.

sections.title: Adult feeding and overwintering
sections.text: My adults preferred apple and other firm fruits. They burrowed in late October and did not feed again until April. I kept the enclosure at approximately 20–24 °C (68–75 °F) through winter. Some adults collected on August 5, 2022, were still alive more than a year later.

sections.title: Offspring
sections.text: The one egg laid before winter produced a male. Breeding activity increased after the adults returned to the surface in spring.

sources.title: Breeding Xyloryctes thestalus at last!!!! (August 25, 2023, updated October 19, 2023)

species.name: Strategus aloeus
species.intro: I reared ox beetles from larvae to adults in less than a year using raised-bed soil. One of my captive-bred males measured 53 mm.

sections.title: Oviposition and larval substrate
sections.text: My females laid eggs in several organic substrates. The larvae developed in raised-bed soil. I recommend firmly compacted topsoil for pupal cells, although development can be completed without it.

sections.title: Adult feeding and longevity
sections.text: I fed the adults every three days. Adult males can live up to two years. My longest-lived female survived approximately nine months.

trials.title: Eastern and western populations
trials.text: I treat the eastern and western populations as two putative species within the Strategus aloeus complex. For the locality assignments, I follow a January 2026 breeding record that placed Arizona and New Mexico stocks in the western group and stocks from western Texas eastward in the eastern group. Breeding lines were kept separately. The locality of my 2022 series was not recorded in the original account.

species.name: Mallodon dasystomus
species.intro: I obtained eggs in a shallow layer of damp hardwood sawdust. The females laid in the sawdust without an intact log.

sections.title: Oviposition
sections.text: I used about 1.3 cm (0.5 in) of damp sawdust in the egg-laying container. The eggs have a hard shell and resemble seeds.

sections.title: Larval development
sections.text: I reared larvae on hardwood sawdust prepared from expanded pellets. Larvae also accept kinshi, a sawdust substrate colonized by fungal mycelium. The larval period ranges from one to three years under different rearing conditions. Larvae accepted supplementary protein and grew rapidly when it was available.

species.name: Stenodontes chevrolati
species.intro: Stenodontes chevrolati is a large prionine longhorn native to southern Florida and parts of the Caribbean. I used to see it only rarely in collections. Captive breeding has made it easier to obtain, and I find it fairly straightforward to rear once I have an active pair. The step I pay closest attention to is separating the young larvae as soon as they hatch.

facts.title: Larval period
facts.text: Usually 1–3 years overall. About 8 months on kinshi in my fastest cultures.

sections.title: Pairing the adults
sections.text: I have never seen my adults feed. They appear to live on reserves accumulated as larvae, and some of mine have lived as long as four months. Once both beetles are active, I introduce the male to the female and watch for mating. My pairs usually mate almost immediately. One mating seems sufficient for the female to lay fertile eggs for the rest of her life. I remove the male afterward because he will keep trying to mate while she is trying to lay.

sections.title: Egg laying and the first galleries
sections.text: For one mated female, I pack raw hardwood sawdust into a container of at least 32 US fl oz (about 0.95 L) and lay a paper towel over the surface. She deposits her eggs on or just below the surface of the sawdust. I expect them to hatch in about a month. The first sign I look for is a set of tiny galleries against the container wall. As soon as I see them, I take the laying box apart and gently sift through the sawdust. I move each hatchling to its own container because the larvae readily cannibalize one another.

sections.title: Choosing a larval substrate
sections.text: I rear each larva in at least 32 fl oz of substrate and prefer a one-gallon jar (3.8 L). I use raw hardwood sawdust, lightly fermented sawdust that has gone through one fermentation, or kinshi, which is sawdust colonized by fungal mycelium. My larvae grew fastest on kinshi, followed by lightly fermented sawdust. On raw sawdust they took about 18–24 months to mature. On kinshi they could reach the same stage in about eight months.

sections.title: Changing food and recognizing pupation
sections.text: With kinshi, I look through the sides of the bottle. When I can no longer see fungus-colonized substrate at the wall, I move the larva to a fresh bottle. With raw or lightly fermented sawdust, I can usually leave the jar for six to eight months between changes. A full-grown larva builds a pupal cell and may spend several months inside. The pupal stage itself lasts about a month. I leave the cell intact and wait for the new adults to become active before introducing another pair.

sources.title: Stenodontes chevrolati breeding account and follow-up, January 21–22, 2026 (Discord)

native_status.text: Native to southern Florida and the Caribbean. Published records include Cuba, the Bahamas and the Cayman Islands. ITIS lists the species as native in the continental United States.

species.name: Dynastes grantii
species.intro: Captive western Hercules beetles pass through three larval instars. A separate longevity record follows a wild-caught Arizona male for more than nine months after collection.

sections.title: Oviposition and larval habitat
sections.text: The captive-rearing account describes oviposition in 15–25 cm of moist substrate. Field records place feeding larvae in rotten wood, including sycamore.

sections.title: Adult longevity
sections.text: A male collected at the Southwestern Research Station in Cochise County, Arizona, on August 20, 2014, survived until May 26, 2015. It remained at room temperature with bark and wood chips, received fresh apple about every four days and remained active through the winter.

sources.title: J. Kim (2015). A rearing guide to Dynastes grantii Horn, 1870. JKim’s Collections.
F.-T. Krell and V. H. I. Krell (2015). Longevity of the western Hercules beetle, Dynastes grantii Horn. The Coleopterists Bulletin 69, 760.
BugGuide, Dynastes grantii. Food and life history.

facts.title: Egg incubation
facts.text: Approximately 2 weeks to 3 months in captive rearing

facts.title: Egg to adult
facts.text: 12–15 months under the reported rearing conditions

facts.title: Adult survival after collection
facts.text: 9 months and 1 week in one Arizona male

trials.title: Captive breeding observations
trials.intro: One female produced 87 eggs in a captive enclosure examined in May 2026. Photographs from other cohorts document variation in developmental timing and the transition from prepupa to pupa.

sections.title: Oviposition
sections.text: On 24 May 2026, 87 eggs were recovered when the enclosure of a single female was examined. The count describes one female.

sections.title: Pupal cell construction
sections.text: In one group, a larva reached the prepupal stage well ahead of its siblings. Another individual began forming a pupal cell in an exhibit enclosure on 23 September 2025. A pupa was photographed in the enclosure on 17 October. Those dates document observations and do not fix the duration of the prepupal stage.

sections.title: Recovery from stored eggs
sections.text: In July 2026, a separate report recorded 12 surviving larvae in a misplaced container that had held more than 80 eggs. The history of the container was incomplete, so the count cannot distinguish failure to hatch from larval mortality.

native_status.text: Native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. The documented range includes Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Chihuahua.

species.name: Euphoria monticola
species.intro: Larvae collected in Arizona reached adulthood and produced one captive generation. The culture was lost after the next generation of larvae was transferred to potting soil.

sections.title: Feeding and oviposition
sections.text: Wild larvae were found beneath decomposing leaf litter. Adults fed at sap flows in the field and accepted fruit and beetle jelly in captivity. The breeding account describes egg laying in flake soil or in a mixture of decayed wood and decomposed leaves. The larvae fed in the same material.

sections.title: Pupation and emergence
sections.text: Larvae constructed cocoons in autumn and remained inside for several months without pupating. After the cocoons were moved to a cold garage for winter, larvae entered the prepupal stage. Pupation followed spring warming, and adults appeared within about a month. The account gives no measured winter temperature.

native_status.text: Native to the southwestern United States and Mexico. The U.S. range includes southeastern Arizona.

species.name: Osmoderma eremicola
species.intro: Second-instar larvae built temporary chambers before resuming growth. Mature third-instar larvae later spent a winter in the cold before pupating. Distinguishing the two periods helps explain the roughly two-year larval cycle reported for this culture.

sections.title: Food and substrate
sections.text: Field observations place larvae in tree cavities and adults at sap flows. Captive adults accepted fruit and beetle jelly. Adults also laid eggs without feeding, but lived for less time and laid fewer eggs. The reported larval substrates were flake soil, decayed wood, or a mixture with well-decomposed hardwood leaves.

sections.title: Larval development
sections.text: Second-instar larvae occupied small chambers for several weeks to a month in summer or autumn. When left undisturbed, they emerged, fed and reached the third instar. The substrate was renewed as larvae consumed it.

sections.title: Overwintering and pupation
sections.text: Mature third instars spent about three months in a garage where winter temperatures were in the low 50s °F (approximately 10–12 °C). Adults emerged close enough together to pair. The pupal cells were fragile and could break when lifted. The culture was left undisturbed during this stage.

native_status.text: Native to eastern North America, including the eastern United States and southern Canada.

sources.title: Steffek et al. (2024), North American Osmoderma
Mountain Lake Biological Station, hermit flower beetle

species.name: Chrysina gloriosa
species.intro: Adults fed on juniper foliage, whereas the larvae developed on decayed hardwood or flake soil. The breeding account describes repeated attempts to maintain successive captive generations.

facts.title: Region in the account
facts.text: Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas

sections.title: Adult feeding and egg laying
sections.text: Fresh juniper cuttings were provided every three days. Eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) was accepted in captivity. Adults fed for several days, then burrowed for about a day before returning to the surface. Eggs were left in the enclosure and hatched there.

sections.title: Larval development
sections.text: The account describes raising larvae on flake soil. Wild larvae develop in decaying hardwood. The captive larvae generally reached the late third instar by autumn.

sections.title: Adult sex characters
sections.text: The terminal abdominal segment in ventral view was more V-shaped in females and more U-shaped in males. A slit at the tip of the terminal segment was visible in males. Males were usually the smaller sex in the culture.

native_status.text: Native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Documented populations include Arizona, western Texas, Chihuahua and Sonora.

sections.title: Pupation
sections.text: A photograph from 31 July documents a pupa of L. placidus, five days after the prepupal observation. The reports do not establish the pupation interval of an individual.

substrate.title: Beetle Substrate Guide
substrate.credit: Flour ratio correction by Leg and Leaf: 15 lb of unbleached flour per 40 lb of sawdust. The original 20 lb batch therefore uses 7.5 lb of flour.

sections.title: Beetle Substrate Guide
sections.subtitle: Lets make this as easy as possible
paragraphs: Here are the very basics: in regards to US native species, Dynastes tityus and granti, Strategus aloeus and antaeus, Gymnetis thula and any Cotinis species, Osmoderma species and Euphoria species can be raised on "Organic Raised Bed Soil" alone! If a larger size is desired, simply mix in raw sawdust! This will be explained in the next slide. But without any mixtures, the organic soil alone will achieve average sized adult beetles!

sections.title: Mixing the Organic Raised Bed Soil
sections.subtitle: Say goodbye to hard to make flake soil!
paragraphs: So if you decide to go down the dark path of ditching flake soil once and for all, but still want that sweet large major male, know that it is still very doable, and easy! Mix in 3/10th of the substrate mass in raw sawdust, you can use any of the hardwood grilling pellets consisting of Oak or Mesquite wood. I personally opt for Mesquite as it is the most affordable option. Make sure the sawdust expands and stir it with the "Organic Raised Bed Soil" throughly. Leave the mixture for two weeks, and stir it whenever you remember to do so (doesn't have to be often). Once the two weeks is up, it is ready for you to add beetles!

A. make sure the organic soil you use do not compose of cow manure. Cow manure contains a bacteria that can cause leg rot with a lot of beetle larvae species and can kill your larvae quickly. That said, most "Organic Raised Bed Soil" purchased from Walmart or Home Depot does not contain cow manure and can be used without issues.
B. This substrate mix is not meant for: any US Lucanid (stag beetles), and any of them Phileurus or Hemiphileurus species.
C. If the intent is to raise large cetoniids (flower beetles), adding a large portion of rotting leaves will also yield desirable results, although raw sawdust works perfectly fine.

sections.title: Making Flake Soil
sections.subtitle: You gotta do it sometime
paragraphs: You really don't have to stress about making flake soil - things ferment in the wild all without human intervention after all. But sometimes, we just gotta speed it up!

sections.title: How to Make Flake Soil
sections.subtitle: Can't be that hard can it?
paragraphs: First up - if you leave raw sawdust by itself in a moist state long enough, certain lucanids will eat it. Yes, you heard me right, the more hardy species will do just fine on aged sawdust. But this might cost you 6 months - a year's time.
So, how do you make flake soil?

Well, you will need ingredients first. 20lbs of hardwood grilling pellets of just about any brand will do the trick for the wood part, but oak and mesquite are your best choices. Then, you need to add 7.5lbs of unbleached flour, and some dry yeast.
The first step is to pour out and expand the pellets with water, and then turn it into sawdust. Warm water works best with this step, but cold will do just fine.

Then you pour the flour into the expanded pellets, along with a table spoon of yeast. You want to mix throughly here, so there isn't huge clumps of flour - an occasional small piece here and there is fine.

The end result should be damp, but not wet. You can check it by squeezing the substrate. It should form a clump and not fall apart when released, all the while having no water come out. If you made it too wet, leave it in somewhere sunny for a few days and stir more often, you will be fine.

Now the waiting game begins. In this stage, you want to mix up the substrate at least once in 2 days (once a day is better). You should notice the substrate heating up, if it does not heat up, simply add more yeast.
It will be about 3 weeks to a month before the soil is ready. Be sure to wait till the substrate is fully cooled down.
Yay, now you have flake soil! The rest of beetle keeping will be a breeze!
